summary: Extends the DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) signal channel with telemetry attributes so a client can share more detail with its DOTS server. These include a baseline of normal traffic, details about attack traffic, and the status of ongoing mitigation. The extra data helps the mitigation provider respond to a distributed denial-of-service attack more effectively. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: When a store is swamped by a mob of fake shoppers, the owner needs to describe what normal days look like and what the mob is doing. This lets the shop send those details to the helpers.

subtitle: How a DDoS mitigation client and server share traffic baselines, attack details and mitigation status over DOTS.

tldr.problem: A DDoS mitigator that knows little about the victim's normal traffic or the attack it faces has to guess, which hurts accuracy and speed. The base DOTS signal channel carries only a mitigation request.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adds optional telemetry to the DOTS signal channel. A client sets up percentile and unit parameters (/tm-setup), reports its normal baseline and pipe capacity, and sends attack details (/tm). Servers can send mitigation status back, and clients can report efficacy.
tldr.outcome: Servers treat the data as hints, so the mitigator can tune itself to the victim and clients can see what the mitigation is doing. A second YANG module lets vendors share attack mapping over the data channel.

today: RFC 9244 is a Standards Track document published in June 2022. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the DOTS signal channel of RFC 9132 and the data channel of RFC 8783, and its telemetry attributes are optional.

sections.title: Telemetry for DOTS
sections.content:
The DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) signal channel (RFC 9132) lets a DOTS client ask a DOTS server to mitigate an attack on a network resource. This RFC adds DOTS telemetry: an optional set of attributes that characterize normal traffic, attacks and mitigation. They are not mandatory parts of the signal channel.

The RFC defines four kinds of information:

  • The normal traffic baseline and the pipe capacity, sent by a client.
  • Attack traffic details, sent by a client in or alongside a mitigation request.
  • Mitigation status attributes, sent by a server to a client.
  • Mitigation efficacy attributes, sent by a client to a server.

It also specifies two YANG modules: one for the telemetry message types and one for sharing attack mapping details over the DOTS data channel (RFC 8783).
sections.eli5: DOTS is a way to call for help when a site is flooded. Telemetry is the extra note you attach: what is normal here, what is going wrong, and how the cleanup is going.

sections.title: Why Share More Detail
sections.content:
The RFC splits DDoS attacks into network- and transport-layer attacks, which aim to overload routers, links and other equipment, and application-layer attacks, which target services such as HTTP, DNS, SIP or SMTP. Attackers often combine several vectors at once and change vectors after a successful mitigation.

Modern detection looks for deviation from a learned normal traffic baseline rather than a fixed threshold. A mitigator cannot learn that baseline during an attack, and the RFC says it is practically impossible for a server's mitigators to compute it with no prior knowledge of the traffic. A client that has calculated its own baseline can pass it on, which is expected to improve time to mitigate, accuracy, and false-negative and false-positive rates.

The server also benefits from the client's view of the attack, and the client benefits from seeing what the server is mitigating. The RFC calls this closing the mitigation loop. Servers must still treat client-provided attack details as hints, since the client and server may classify attacks differently.

A third need is the total pipe capacity, the traffic level the client domain can absorb from upstream. A mitigator that returns a lot of supposedly clean traffic could saturate that pipe, so the server can use a mechanism such as the rate-limit action of RFC 8783.
sections.eli5: A helper who knows what a normal day looks like can spot trouble faster. And if you tell the helper how wide your doorway is, they will not push more people through it than it can handle.

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.content:
DOTS has two channels. The signal channel must work even while attack traffic saturates links, so its messages are kept small. The data channel is for bulk transfer before or after an attack. Most telemetry goes in the signal channel, because ongoing attack and baseline data must be delivered during an attack. Only the attack mapping tables use the data channel.

Telemetry messages are encoded in CBOR, and the YANG module in Section 11.1 provides the data model and encoding rules, not NETCONF or RESTCONF management of the server. The module uses enumerations instead of identities to keep messages compact.

Two new operation paths are added:

  • /tm-setup for telemetry setup (Section 7).
  • /tm for pre-or-ongoing-mitigation telemetry (Section 8).

Implementations MUST support the Observe Option (RFC 7641) for /tm. Large transfers can use CoAP block-wise options (RFC 7959), but Block1 transfers are likely to fail if the inbound pipe is full, so the RFC advises fitting a request into a single packet or splitting it into several that each fit. Setup requests and responses are Confirmable CoAP messages, while telemetry requests and responses are Non-confirmable.
sections.eli5: There is a small, tough walkie-talkie for emergencies and a big truck for heavy deliveries. Most of the notes go on the walkie-talkie, because it still works in a storm. Only the big reference books ride the truck.

sections.title: Telemetry Setup
sections.content:
Before sending data, a client can configure telemetry with PUT requests on /tm-setup. A setup message carries only one of three things: telemetry configuration, pipe capacity, or baseline information. A request mixing them is rejected with 4.00 (Bad Request).

Configuration. Telemetry describes traffic by a few percentiles taken from sampling buckets across a measurement interval. The defaults are the 10th (low), 50th (mid) and 90th (high) percentiles plus the peak (100th). A client can change them, or disable one by setting it to 0.00. It also picks unit classes (packets, bits or bytes per second) and can set server-originated-telemetry to true to ask for telemetry from the server. A GET on /tm-setup returns the min and max values the server accepts.

Pipe capacity. A list of ingress links, each with a link-id, a capacity and a unit. The client auto-scales to the largest unit that gives a value greater than one, and a link is removed by sending capacity 0.

Baseline. Normal traffic percentiles for a target, in total, per protocol and per port. Optional connection-capacity limits can also be sent, such as maximum simultaneous connections, embryonic connections, connections per second, requests per second and outstanding partial requests.

Each setup carries a Telemetry Setup Identifier, tsid, generated by the client in the Uri-Path. It MUST increase monotonically, and a higher tsid overrides a lower one for the same data. A server must not expect refreshes, and setup stays valid until it stops serving the client domain. A DELETE without tsid resets everything to defaults. If two clients of one domain send conflicting pipe or baseline data, the server reports a conflict, with cause code 5 for overlapping pipe scope.
sections.eli5: First you fill in a short form: how many slices to cut the day into, what size of traffic to report, and how wide the doorway is. Each new form gets a bigger number so the helper knows which one is the latest.

sections.title: Telemetry During Mitigation
sections.content:
Attack-time telemetry is sent with PUT on /tm. Each message is identified by a client-generated Telemetry Identifier, tmid, which also increases monotonically. A message must include a target (identified by prefix, FQDN, URI, alias name or a pointer to a mitigation request through mid-list) and at least one other attribute. Agents SHOULD bind telemetry to the mitigation requests for the resources under attack. They MUST NOT send notifications to the same peer more often than the telemetry-notify-interval.

The pre-or-ongoing-mitigation attributes are:

  • total-traffic, by protocol and by port, with percentiles, peak and current values.
  • total-attack-traffic, also by protocol and by port.
  • total-attack-connection values for resource-consuming attacks: connections, embryonic connections, connections per second, requests per second and partial requests.
  • attack-detail, covered in the next section.

Server to client. A server can send attack details to a client that enabled server-originated-telemetry during setup. The client sends a PUT with a target filter and then a GET with Observe set to 0, optionally filtered with Uri-Query parameters, to receive asynchronous notifications. Servers MUST NOT include telemetry attributes in status updates for sessions where that flag is false.

Mitigation updates. A client can include total attack traffic and attack details in its periodic efficacy updates, and a server can include total traffic, attack connections, attack traffic and attack details in its mitigation status updates. The RFC recommends that the client first establish a telemetry setup session during idle time, which also reveals whether the server supports telemetry.

Errors add to those of RFC 9132. A request that violates the extension or has invalid query types gets 4.00 (Bad Request), and an unknown tsid or tmid, or a target query that does not match the mitigation, gets 4.04 (Not Found).
sections.eli5: During the emergency, you radio in what you see: how much traffic is coming, how much of it is bad, and which part of the building is hit. The helper can radio back what they are blocking.

sections.title: Attack Details and Vendor Mapping
sections.content:
An attack-detail entry is keyed by vendor-id (the security vendor's IANA Private Enterprise Number) and an attack-id assigned by that vendor. The attack-id MUST always be present. Optional sub-attributes include a text attack-description (with a language tag, default en-US), an attack-severity taken from RFC 7970, start-time and end-time in seconds since 1970, a source-count with percentile values, and a top-talker list.

Each top talker has a source prefix, optional source port and ICMP type ranges, a spoofed-status (unknown if omitted, which matters for reflection attacks), and its own attack traffic or connection statistics.

Vendors describe attacks differently, so the RFC uses text descriptions instead of trying to standardize attack types. To save space during an attack, mapping tables from attack-id to description can be installed in advance over the data channel with the second YANG module, ietf-dots-mapping. An agent MUST accept telemetry with a vendor identifier different from the one it uses, and SHOULD send telemetry using the vendor mappings it has provided to its peer.
sections.eli5: Each security company has its own names for kinds of attacks. So the report carries the company's number and a short description, and a lookup list can be handed over before trouble starts.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Telemetry reveals the client network's topology, pipe capacity, normal traffic baseline, connection capacity, and threat and mitigation information. The RFC calls this sensitive and says the DOTS server domain MUST protect it at rest. Sharing it with a trusted server adds no significant new concern beyond that, since such a server is already trusted by being able to observe and mitigate attacks.

A compromised DOTS client can send fake telemetry to mislead a server. The RFC suggests monitoring and auditing clients and authorizing each only for specific target resources. Servers must also defend against denial-of-service attempts by compromised clients, for example by limiting the probing rate, rate-limiting telemetry (including requests that keep using new tmid values), and enforcing a quota and time limit on active tmid items.

For the vendor mapping module, writable nodes are sensitive: a bad mapping would mislead the server when it correlates attack details. Readable mapping data could expose which DDoS protection technology a client domain uses, or be leaked by a compromised client to reveal the server's detection capabilities.
sections.eli5: The note you send tells the helper about your building's weak spots, so it must be kept private. And a pretend helper or a lying note could cause trouble, so both sides check who is allowed to say what.

items.desc: The tsid already existed and the update was accepted.

items.label: Deleted
items.desc: Reply to a DELETE, even if the tsid did not exist.

items.label: Bad Request
items.desc: Missing or invalid parameters, or a mix of configuration, pipe and baseline data.

items.label: Not Found
items.desc: A GET named a tsid the server does not have.

items.desc: A value is not acceptable to the server; the client may retry.
